Based on my research, I can identify the president you're looking for.

The answer is **Martin Van Buren**.

Let me verify each qualification:

1. **Democratic president**: ✅ Yes, Van Buren was a member of the Democratic Party (he was instrumental in founding the modern Democratic Party).

2. **Served only one term **(as of 2024): ✅ Yes, Van Buren served exactly one four-year term from March 4, 1837 to March 4, 1841. He was defeated by William Henry Harrison in the 1840 election and never ran for president again.

3. **Signed 10 or fewer executive orders**: ✅ Yes, according to historical records, Martin Van Buren signed exactly **10 executive orders** during his presidency—matching your upper limit precisely.

4. **No wars declared during his presidency**: ✅ Yes, no formal declarations of war occurred during Van Buren's time in office. While there were tensions such as the Aroostook War (a border dispute with Britain over Maine) and ongoing Seminole conflicts in Florida, neither resulted in a congressional declaration of war. Van Buren successfully maintained peace with Great Britain through diplomatic resolution (the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842).

Martin Van Buren is the eighth U.S. President who meets all four of your criteria.

The form, substance and numbers of presidential orders _(jump to table below)_ has varied dramatically in the history of the US Presidency. Numbering of Executive Orders began in 1907 by the Department of State, which assigned numbers to all the orders in their files, dating from 1862 (Lord 1944, viii). Through those efforts, the frequency of unnumbered orders declined sharply. President Hoover attempted to bring further order and regularity to the processing and documenting of Executive orders (ibid).
But it was not until the Federal Register Act in 1936 that a more thorough contemporaneous documentation of Executive Orders began. Before then, and occasionally afterwards, discovery of an order not previously counted has resulted in assigning a number already in use together with an associated letter (e.g., 7709, 7709-A). This practice explains why the total number of orders issued may be greater than the result that would be obtained by subtracting a president’s first order number from his last (and adding 1).
Today virtually all numbered Executive Orders are published. However, the Federal Register Act specified that such orders need not be published if they had “no general applicability and legal effect.” Thus, the text of some post-1936 orders is not generally available--but we think we have all of them at the APP.
In addition to the numbered executive orders, there are many unnumbered orders (see Lord 1943). The best known compilation includes “over 1500” unnumbered orders, but the editor notes that the true total is unknown. Estimates have reportedly ranged as high as 50,000. The editor, Lord, notes emphatically that “no distinction can be made between numbered and unnumbered Orders on the basis of subject matter, general applicability, public interest, or legal effect.”
There have always been many forms of Presidential orders in addition to the numbered Executive Orders and Executive Orders included in the published "unnumbered series". Currently, these commonly are called “Memorandums” but can have many titles. Decades ago, such documents were commonly titled “Letters.”

**In this table we present the total number of Executive Orders issued by presidential term (not calendar year). Thus, _this table does not include other forms of written presidential orders(such as memorandums), or discretionary executive actions not accompanied by a published presidential directive_.**For an illustration of the many different kinds of presidential directives that are NOT called "Executive Orders" see our Analysis "Biden in Action." For further illustrations of the problems involved in simply counting documents, see another Analysis looking at presidential use of discretion in the first two years of elected presidents starting with Nixon.
The table below is modified and updated from time to time. This table includes our own original tallies for the first FDR term based on Lord (1943, 1944). Our numbers still differ slightly from the numbers posted in the NARA Executive Order Disposition Tables. But we are confident that we have correctly counted the Lord entries (and the NARA figures are very close to ours).
Our APP document collection of numbered Executive Orders is complete with respect to published Orders starting in 1945. We are adding earlier orders to the collection as possible, and welcome (and will gladly acknowledge) contributions to this effort. We will also be adding our independent tallies for unnumbered orders.

This page is a list of Executive orders which have been issued by the Office of the President of the United States of America (POTUS) to give specific presidential policy and implementation directions to officers and agencies of this country's Executive branch. Federal government offices and agencies are required to follow the directions of such Executive orders, within the limits of existing federal laws passed by the United States Congress and defined by the Constitution of the United States, as interpreted by the Judicial branch of the federal government.
At the federal level of government in the United States, laws are made almost exclusively by legislation. Such legislation originates as an act of Congress passed by the U.S. Congress; such acts were either signed into law by the president or passed by Congress after a presidential veto.
Legislation is not the only source of law. There is also judge-made common law and constitutional law. The president can also issue executive orders pursuant to a grant of discretion from Congress, or under the inherent powers that office holds to deal with certain matters which have the force of law.
Many early executive orders were not recorded. The State Department began numbering executive orders in the early 20th century, starting retroactively from President Abraham Lincoln's Executive Order Establishing a Provisional Court in Louisiana issued in 1862.

The form, substance and numbers of presidential orders _(jump to table below)_ has varied dramatically in the history of the US Presidency. Numbering of Executive Orders began in 1907 by the Department of State, which assigned numbers to all the orders in their files, dating from 1862 (Lord 1944, viii). Through those efforts, the frequency of unnumbered orders declined sharply. President Hoover attempted to bring further order and regularity to the processing and documenting of Executive orders (ibid).
But it was not until the Federal Register Act in 1936 that a more thorough contemporaneous documentation of Executive Orders began. Before then, and occasionally afterwards, discovery of an order not previously counted has resulted in assigning a number already in use together with an associated letter (e.g., 7709, 7709-A). This practice explains why the total number of orders issued may be greater than the result that would be obtained by subtracting a president’s first order number from his last (and adding 1).
Today virtually all numbered Executive Orders are published. However, the Federal Register Act specified that such orders need not be published if they had “no general applicability and legal effect.” Thus, the text of some post-1936 orders is not generally available--but we think we have all of them at the APP.
In addition to the numbered executive orders, there are many unnumbered orders (see Lord 1943). The best known compilation includes “over 1500” unnumbered orders, but the editor notes that the true total is unknown. Estimates have reportedly ranged as high as 50,000. The editor, Lord, notes emphatically that “no distinction can be made between numbered and unnumbered Orders on the basis of subject matter, general applicability, public interest, or legal effect.”
There have always been many forms of Presidential orders in addition to the numbered Executive Orders and Executive Orders included in the published "unnumbered series". Currently, these commonly are called “Memorandums” but can have many titles. Decades ago, such documents were commonly titled “Letters.”

Martin Van Buren's tenure as the eighth president of the United States began on March 4, 1837, and ended on March 4, 1841. Van Buren, a Democrat and vice president under Andrew Jackson, took office after defeating multiple Whig Party candidates in the 1836 presidential election. Van Buren's presidency ended following his defeat by Whig candidate William Henry Harrison in the 1840 presidential election.
The central issue facing President Van Buren was the Panic of 1837, a sustained economic downturn that began just weeks into his presidency. Van Buren opposed any direct federal government intervention and cut back federal spending to maintain a balanced budget. He also presided over the establishment of the independent treasury system, a series of government vaults that replaced banks as the repository of federal funds. Van Buren continued the Indian removal policies of the Jackson administration, as thousands of Native Americans were resettled west of the Mississippi River during his presidency. He sought to avoid major tensions over slavery, rejecting the possibility of annexing Texas and appealing the case of _United States v. The Amistad_ to the Supreme Court. In foreign affairs, Van Buren avoided war with Britain despite several incidents, including the bloodless Aroostook War and the _Caroline_ Affair.
Van Buren's inability to deal effectively with the economic depression, combined with the growing political strength of the opposition Whigs, led to his defeat in the 1840 presidential election. His presidency was marked as much by failure and criticism as by success and popular acclaim, and is often ranked as average or below-average by historians. His most lasting achievement was as a political organizer who built the modern Democratic Party and guided it to dominance in the new Second Party System.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole16-1)

## Presidential election of 1836
[edit]
Van Buren had emerged as President Andrew Jackson's preferred successor during the Petticoat affair, and Van Buren won election as vice president in 1832.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson19849%E2%80%9310-2) The two men –charismatic "Old Hickory" and the super-efficient "Sly Fox"—had entirely different personalities but had become an effective team in eight years in office together.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-3) Jackson declined to seek another term in the 1836 presidential election, but he remained influential within the Democratic Party, and he strongly supported Van Buren's candidacy in the 1836 election.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-4) With Jackson's support, Van Buren won the presidential nomination of the 1835 Democratic National Convention without opposition.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-5) Two names were put forward for the vice-presidential nomination: Representative Richard M. Johnson of Kentucky, and former senator William Cabell Rives of Virginia. Though most Southern Democrats favored Rives, Jackson preferred Johnson, and his influence helped lead to Johnson's nomination for the vice presidency.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-5)
1836 electoral vote results

## Presidential election of 1836
The newly established Whig Party, a loose coalition bound by mutual opposition to Jackson, sought to prevent Van Buren's victory in the election of 1836. Lacking the party unity or organizational strength to field a single ticket or define a single platform, the Whigs fielded multiple candidates in the hope of forcing a contingent election in the House of Representatives.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-6) Senator Hugh Lawson White of Tennessee, a former Jackson ally, emerged as the major Whig candidate in the South, touting himself as the only Southerner in the race. William Henry Harrison, who had gained notoriety for his service in the Battle of Tippecanoe, edged out Senator Daniel Webster to become the main Whig candidate in the North.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2005448%E2%80%93449-7) The Whig Party campaigned on denouncing Jackson's alleged executive tyranny, and attacked Van Buren as an untrustworthy career politician.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2005449%E2%80%93450-8)

## Presidential election of 1836
Van Buren had to articulate a position on slavery that could win full-throated approval in both the pro-slavery South and the Northern states where slavery was illegal and unpopular. The biggest challenge came in the South, where all Yankees were automatically suspect on the slave question.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-9) Van Buren moved to obtain the support of Southerners by assuring them that he opposed abolitionism and supported the continued existence of slavery in states where it was present.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2007508%E2%80%93509-10) Van Buren did not discuss his own personal beliefs, which held that slavery was immoral, but was sanctioned by the Constitution.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-11) Van Buren's strategy was not to defend his personal position, but to attack abolitionists, who were popular nowhere in the United States. As vice president, he cast the tie-breaking Senate vote in favor of a bill to subject abolitionist mail to state laws, thus ensuring that abolitionist mail would not be circulated in the South. While Southern Whigs cast doubt on his devotion to slavery, his supporters insisted he believed in three things: that Congress could not interfere with slavery in the states, that it would be "impolitic" to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, and that agitation about slavery endangered the union. Van Buren and his supporters realized that to build a viable national party and to maintain the union they had to compromise by accepting slavery. The Democrats created the first modern party, but in doing so consciously removed slavery and abolition from the partisan agenda. More than a decade later, in 1848, Van Buren would become a leading opponent of the extension of slavery in the North while running with the Free Soil Party, but by then he had abandoned any hope of Southern support.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-12)

In his posthumously published memoirs, Martin Van Buren covered his rise in New York politics and his subsequent contributions to the formation of the Democratic Party and Andrew Jackson’s presidency. It seems symbolic, however, that the memoirs never reached his own presidential administration, depriving Americans of Van Buren’s self-assessment of his time as chief executive. In much the same way, scholars focus on his pre-presidential enterprises as the peak of his political career, with Van Buren’s presidency a disappointing coda best forgotten.
Van Buren’s life, however, was more than the high of building a political party, more than the low of having his presidential agenda derailed by an economic depression. His story was one of talent, hard work, ambition, success, personal loss, failure, false hope, betrayal, and sadness. In other words, Van Buren lived the range of human experience, making his life a reminder that despite the power and prestige they hold, presidents are regular people, too.
Martin Van Buren was a one-term president whose administration faced significant challenges and produced mixed results at best. His mark on U.S. history was about more than those four years, though. He was the most significant figure in creating the Democratic Party and in setting the expectations for electoral competition based on two opposing political parties. Politics in the United States would look very differently today without his contributions.

#### Politician on the Rise
Born in 1782, Van Buren was the first president born after the American Revolution and the first not descended from the British. He was raised in Columbia County, New York, an area largely populated by people of Dutch ancestry, like the Van Burens, and supportive of the Federalists. Martin’s father, Abraham, was a Jeffersonian Republican, and his son followed in his footsteps.
Martin Van Buren became a lawyer and worked his way up in New York state politics, dominated at the time by the likes of Aaron Burr and DeWitt Clinton. Van Buren spent time in the New York state senate, then was appointed as the state’s attorney general. By the time he entered the U.S. Senate in late 1821, Van Buren had organized an impressive group of New York politicians later dubbed the Albany Regency.
After supporting William H. Crawford’s unsuccessful presidential candidacy in 1824, Van Buren put together a national political coalition that became the Democratic Party. This coalition threw its weight behind Andrew Jackson in 1828, helping him win the presidency. Jackson rewarded Van Buren, recently elected as New York’s governor, by appointing him U.S. secretary of state.
Van Buren proved to be adept at foreign relations. More importantly for his future political career, he was also the president’s staunchest ally in the cabinet. When internal dissension over the marriage of one of Jackson’s cabinet secretaries, Secretary of War John Eaton, threatened to tear the cabinet apart, Van Buren sacrificed his position by resigning. His immediate reward was a diplomatic appointment to London. More important was Jackson’s endorsement to become his vice president if he won reelection in 1832, which Jackson did. This decision positioned Van Buren to succeed him at the end of his second term. Van Buren spent most of his time as vice president advising Jackson on the Bank War, the president’s effort to close the Second Bank of the United States.

#### A Disappointing Presidency
After defeating his Whig opponents in the 1836 presidential election, Van Buren intended to continue enacting Jackson’s political agenda. He was able to do so in some cases. Van Buren oversaw the removal of the Cherokee Indians via the Trail of Tears and persisted in prosecuting the war against the Seminole Indians in Florida. He also continued supporting the institution of slavery in a bid to retain the political support of white southerners. Like Jackson, Van Buren also deferred a decision on the annexation of Texas.
The onset of the 1837 economic depression shortly after Van Buren took office, however, presented him with unexpected challenges. The changed economic circumstances facing the nation forced him to spend considerable time looking for a solution that would provide financial stability. Congress did not implement Van Buren’s proposal—housing federal dollars in an independent Treasury rather than a national bank or state banks—until the last year of his presidency when it passed the Independent Treasury Act of 1840.
Other circumstances provided Van Buren with the opportunity to prove his political acumen as chief executive. Conflicts along the U.S.-Canadian border threatened to ignite a yet another war with Great Britain. Van Buren refused to be provoked into taking aggressive military action, instead relying on diplomacy to defuse the tension. When asked to assist the Mormons in their request for compensation for property lost due to religious persecution, however, Van Buren chose to protect his electoral chances rather than provide them with support.

#### Political Defeat and Retirement
The 1840 presidential campaign exposed Van Buren’s (and the Democratic Party’s) many weaknesses. The Whig Party had spent the years since the last presidential election organizing its members in formidable ways, embracing the cultural politics—material, print, and visual culture, political events and music, public correspondence, auxiliary organizations, and women’s political activity—that Van Buren and many Democrats had never fully activated on a national scale. The Whigs were able to hammer the president on his weak, ineffective response to the economic depression and its effects on the American people.
The Whigs nominated a military hero, William Henry Harrison, and constructed an image of him as an ordinary farmer who understood the plight facing everyday Americans. Meanwhile, they portrayed Van Buren as an out-of-touch elitist living in luxury while average Americans suffered. Neither image was correct—Harrison came from wealth, while Van Buren did not—but in politics, perception often trumps reality.
Although Van Buren lost the 1840 presidential election, he was not yet done with presidential politics. He went into the 1844 Democratic National Convention as the favored candidate, but his opposition to immediately allowing Texas to join the United States sunk his chances of receiving the party’s presidential nomination. Then Van Buren’s attempt to influence President James Polk’s cabinet selections failed, leading to a break between the two men that was never repaired.
Four years later in 1848, the antislavery Free Soil Party nominated Van Buren to head its ticket. It was an odd political partnership given Van Buren’s leadership in the Democratic Party that he had founded and his historical support for slavery, and it showed in the ineffectiveness of his campaign.
Van Buren went back to the Democratic Party after 1848, acting as its elder statesman. With the help of two sons and a daughter-in-law, he worked on his memoirs and a study of U.S. political parties. He died at his home in Kinderhook, New York, in 1862.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
Martin Van Buren, photographed sometime between 1860 and 1862.
Martin Van Buren was the 8th President of the United States, in office from March 4, 1837, through March 4, 1841. Widely regarded as a talented politician, Van Buren was known to contemporaries as "**the Little Magician**" for his political acumen. Despite entering the presidency as a generally popular figure, Van Buren's presidency was hampered by a major economic downturn.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### Early Life and New York Politics
Martin Van Buren was born on December 5, 1782, in Kinderhook, New York, near the end of the American Revolution. As a result, he later became the first U.S. president born after American independence, and the first not born a British subject. His Dutch ancestry also made him the first president of non-British descent.
Van Buren attended school until the age of fourteen before becoming a law clerk in 1796. After completing his law studies in New York City, he gained admission to the bar in 1803. Thereafter, Van Buren returned to Kinderhook, where he opened a successful law practice with his half-brother, James J. Van Alen.
During this time, Van Buren became active in New York politics. Though the Federalists (one of the major political parties of the era) were dominant in New York, Van Buren gravitated towards the views of the rival Democratic-Republicans (the party of Thomas Jefferson). Throughout his political career, he remained committed to Jeffersonian principles of limited government and the protection of states' rights.
Elected to the New York State Senate in 1812, and appointed state Attorney General in 1815, Van Buren found himself in frequent conflict with New York Federalists throughout the 1810s. He nonetheless became a powerful force in state politics and won both praise and criticism for his skill at political maneuvering. Early in the 1820s, Van Buren came to head the **Albany Regency**, a powerful party machine that further increased his power in the state.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### National Politics and the Founding of the Democratic Party
In 1821, Van Buren won election to the United States Senate from New York. Despite his junior status, his political acumen quickly allowed him to become a prominent figure in national politics. Van Buren was rapidly appointed to the Senate finance committee, and he soon became chairman of the judiciary committee.
Following the election of John Quincy Adams in 1824, Van Buren became a vocal critic of the President, whom he saw as striving to expand the power of the federal government. With an eye towards the election of 1828, Van Buren worked to unite many different factions of the Democratic-Republican party in support of war hero **Andrew Jackson**. This coalition-building effort ultimately resulted in the election of Jackson in 1828 and marked the beginning of the modern-day **Democratic Party**.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### Martin Van Buren and the Administration of Andrew Jackson
Despite his national profile, Van Buren remained a political force in New York State during the 1820s, and in 1828 he successfully ran for Governor of New York. However, while he assumed the governorship in January 1829, he only held it for a few weeks before being selected by Andrew Jackson to become the Secretary of State.
The years of the Jackson presidency were highly tumultuous, and during his first term, Jackson faced serious divisions within his cabinet. During this time, Van Buren became one of President Jackson's closest advisors and friends. Additionally, as Secretary of State, he had several notable accomplishments. These included gaining reparations from France for property seized during the Napoleonic Wars and negotiating a treaty with the Ottoman Empire that allowed American traders access to the Black Sea.
Eventually, divisions within Jackson's cabinet reached a boiling point. Van Buren devised a scheme whereby he would resign, giving Jackson political cover to remove the rest of his cabinet. Jackson agreed to this plan, but subsequently appointed Van Buren as U.S. Minister to Great Britain in 1831.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### The Path to the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's first term, one of the major sources of division within the cabinet was Vice-President John C. Calhoun. As a result, as Jackson prepared his reelection campaign in 1832, he selected Van Buren to replace Calhoun as his running mate. Jackson easily won reelection.
As Vice-President, much of Van Buren's focus was on "the Bank War"—the Jackson administration's fight with the Second Bank of the United States. This conflict involved Jackson's desire to prevent the recharter of the Bank, which he felt benefited too few wealthy Americans at the expense of the masses. The Bank War helped to rearrange the American political parties of the era. Jackson's opposition coalesced into the Whig Party, while Jackson and Van Buren continued to play key roles in the shaping of the Democratic Party.
As the election of 1836 approached, Jackson made Van Buren his chosen successor. Van Buren, in turn, made it clear that he intended to continue Jackson's policies. With the support of a by-then well-defined Democratic Party, Van Buren defeated three Whig candidates who ran against him, securing more votes than all three combined.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
A portrait of Martin Van Buren near the time of his presidency.
Despite his popularity upon taking office, the Presidency of Martin Van Buren would only last for one term. During his time in office, Van Buren found himself hindered by a major economic crisis. Still, "the Little Magician" managed a number of key accomplishments, mostly in the realm of foreign affairs.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### The Panic of 1837 and the Independent Treasury Act
Almost immediately upon assuming the presidency, Van Buren was confronted with a major economic crisis known as the **Panic of 1837**. While historians still debate the exact cause of the Panic, in large part, it was related to policy actions taken by Jackson during the earlier Bank War.
Desiring to remain true to his belief in the principle of limited government, Van Buren's proposed response to the Panic of 1837 was to establish an independent treasury that he hoped would stabilize the American economy by separating federal funding from state banks. The plan drew strong opposition from both Whigs and Van Buren's own party, the Democrats. Eventually, Congress authorized the creation of a Treasury. However, by the time the Independent Treasury Act of 1840 was passed, the economy had been in a depression for almost four years. This, more than any other factor, cost Van Buren in the election of 1840.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### Other Domestic Affairs During the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's second term, Congress had passed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 to legalize the forcible relocation of all Native American peoples to the west of the Mississippi. Van Buren continued this policy. During his time in office, the federal government both oversaw a forced relocation of the Cherokee people and contended with a major uprising of Seminole peoples in Florida. Both events resulted in the deaths of thousands of Native Americans. Van Buren's handling of the Seminole uprising in particular was criticized as inhumane and contributed to the erosion of his popularity.
Van Buren was also confronted with issues related to sectional tensions over slavery. In 1837, he announced that he would not support the annexation of the Mexican territory of Texas. The annexation of Texas would have brought another state that permitted slavery into the Union, and Van Buren's rejection of that possibility did help to calm temporarily tensions over the issue.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### Foreign Affairs During the Martin Van Buren Presidency
A major source of pressure during the Van Buren administration was American relations with Great Britain. As a result, Van Buren faced a succession of diplomatic crises during his four years in office.
In 1837, a Canadian separatist movement attempted to seize independence from Great Britain. When they were unsuccessful, they took refuge in the United States and recruited a number of Americans to support them. The conflict eventually resulted in the death of an American citizen when British loyalists seized and sank a ship supplying the rebels, who based themselves on an island in the Niagara River.
Van Buren sought to avoid escalating tensions with Great Britain, despite domestic calls to declare war. To try and secure a peaceful resolution to the situation, he dispatched General Winfield Scott to the Niagara region to make it clear to any Americans fighting against the British that they would not be supported by the federal government. Also, he declared American neutrality regarding the Canadian independence issue.
While these actions managed to calm the situation, another crisis broke out in 1838, when American and British forces began to clash along a disputed border in northern Maine. To deescalate what was known as the Aroostook War, Van Buren personally agreed with the British minister to the United States to reach a diplomatic solution. He also dispatched General Winfield Scott to calm tensions in the region. Although he had left office by the time of its signing, the 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty resolved the border issues and was the result of the diplomatic process started by Van Buren.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Election of 1840 and Martin Van Buren's Later Years
As the election of 1840 approached, Van Buren faced declining favorability across the country. Many were upset at his handling of the economic crisis, others disagreed with his diplomatic approach to dealing with the British, and still others found fault with his handling of slavery concerns. Indeed, in an attempt to earn the support for pro-slavery voices after his refusal to annex Texas, in 1839 Van Buren's administration supported returning the Africans on trial for engaging in mutiny aboard the slave ship _Amistad_ to Spanish authorities. However, the Supreme Court later ruled that the captives had acted in self-defense and ordered their release.

Martin Van Buren, photographed sometime between 1860 and 1862.
Martin Van Buren was the 8th President of the United States, in office from March 4, 1837, through March 4, 1841. Widely regarded as a talented politician, Van Buren was known to contemporaries as "**the Little Magician**" for his political acumen. Despite entering the presidency as a generally popular figure, Van Buren's presidency was hampered by a major economic downturn.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### Early Life and New York Politics
Martin Van Buren was born on December 5, 1782, in Kinderhook, New York, near the end of the American Revolution. As a result, he later became the first U.S. president born after American independence, and the first not born a British subject. His Dutch ancestry also made him the first president of non-British descent.
Van Buren attended school until the age of fourteen before becoming a law clerk in 1796. After completing his law studies in New York City, he gained admission to the bar in 1803. Thereafter, Van Buren returned to Kinderhook, where he opened a successful law practice with his half-brother, James J. Van Alen.
During this time, Van Buren became active in New York politics. Though the Federalists (one of the major political parties of the era) were dominant in New York, Van Buren gravitated towards the views of the rival Democratic-Republicans (the party of Thomas Jefferson). Throughout his political career, he remained committed to Jeffersonian principles of limited government and the protection of states' rights.
Elected to the New York State Senate in 1812, and appointed state Attorney General in 1815, Van Buren found himself in frequent conflict with New York Federalists throughout the 1810s. He nonetheless became a powerful force in state politics and won both praise and criticism for his skill at political maneuvering. Early in the 1820s, Van Buren came to head the **Albany Regency**, a powerful party machine that further increased his power in the state.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### National Politics and the Founding of the Democratic Party
In 1821, Van Buren won election to the United States Senate from New York. Despite his junior status, his political acumen quickly allowed him to become a prominent figure in national politics. Van Buren was rapidly appointed to the Senate finance committee, and he soon became chairman of the judiciary committee.
Following the election of John Quincy Adams in 1824, Van Buren became a vocal critic of the President, whom he saw as striving to expand the power of the federal government. With an eye towards the election of 1828, Van Buren worked to unite many different factions of the Democratic-Republican party in support of war hero **Andrew Jackson**. This coalition-building effort ultimately resulted in the election of Jackson in 1828 and marked the beginning of the modern-day **Democratic Party**.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### Martin Van Buren and the Administration of Andrew Jackson
Despite his national profile, Van Buren remained a political force in New York State during the 1820s, and in 1828 he successfully ran for Governor of New York. However, while he assumed the governorship in January 1829, he only held it for a few weeks before being selected by Andrew Jackson to become the Secretary of State.
The years of the Jackson presidency were highly tumultuous, and during his first term, Jackson faced serious divisions within his cabinet. During this time, Van Buren became one of President Jackson's closest advisors and friends. Additionally, as Secretary of State, he had several notable accomplishments. These included gaining reparations from France for property seized during the Napoleonic Wars and negotiating a treaty with the Ottoman Empire that allowed American traders access to the Black Sea.
Eventually, divisions within Jackson's cabinet reached a boiling point. Van Buren devised a scheme whereby he would resign, giving Jackson political cover to remove the rest of his cabinet. Jackson agreed to this plan, but subsequently appointed Van Buren as U.S. Minister to Great Britain in 1831.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### The Path to the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's first term, one of the major sources of division within the cabinet was Vice-President John C. Calhoun. As a result, as Jackson prepared his reelection campaign in 1832, he selected Van Buren to replace Calhoun as his running mate. Jackson easily won reelection.
As Vice-President, much of Van Buren's focus was on "the Bank War"—the Jackson administration's fight with the Second Bank of the United States. This conflict involved Jackson's desire to prevent the recharter of the Bank, which he felt benefited too few wealthy Americans at the expense of the masses. The Bank War helped to rearrange the American political parties of the era. Jackson's opposition coalesced into the Whig Party, while Jackson and Van Buren continued to play key roles in the shaping of the Democratic Party.
As the election of 1836 approached, Jackson made Van Buren his chosen successor. Van Buren, in turn, made it clear that he intended to continue Jackson's policies. With the support of a by-then well-defined Democratic Party, Van Buren defeated three Whig candidates who ran against him, securing more votes than all three combined.

A portrait of Martin Van Buren near the time of his presidency.
Despite his popularity upon taking office, the Presidency of Martin Van Buren would only last for one term. During his time in office, Van Buren found himself hindered by a major economic crisis. Still, "the Little Magician" managed a number of key accomplishments, mostly in the realm of foreign affairs.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### The Panic of 1837 and the Independent Treasury Act
Almost immediately upon assuming the presidency, Van Buren was confronted with a major economic crisis known as the **Panic of 1837**. While historians still debate the exact cause of the Panic, in large part, it was related to policy actions taken by Jackson during the earlier Bank War.
Desiring to remain true to his belief in the principle of limited government, Van Buren's proposed response to the Panic of 1837 was to establish an independent treasury that he hoped would stabilize the American economy by separating federal funding from state banks. The plan drew strong opposition from both Whigs and Van Buren's own party, the Democrats. Eventually, Congress authorized the creation of a Treasury. However, by the time the Independent Treasury Act of 1840 was passed, the economy had been in a depression for almost four years. This, more than any other factor, cost Van Buren in the election of 1840.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### Other Domestic Affairs During the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's second term, Congress had passed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 to legalize the forcible relocation of all Native American peoples to the west of the Mississippi. Van Buren continued this policy. During his time in office, the federal government both oversaw a forced relocation of the Cherokee people and contended with a major uprising of Seminole peoples in Florida. Both events resulted in the deaths of thousands of Native Americans. Van Buren's handling of the Seminole uprising in particular was criticized as inhumane and contributed to the erosion of his popularity.
Van Buren was also confronted with issues related to sectional tensions over slavery. In 1837, he announced that he would not support the annexation of the Mexican territory of Texas. The annexation of Texas would have brought another state that permitted slavery into the Union, and Van Buren's rejection of that possibility did help to calm temporarily tensions over the issue.

# Presidency of Martin Van Buren | Major Events & Accomplishments
## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### Foreign Affairs During the Martin Van Buren Presidency
A major source of pressure during the Van Buren administration was American relations with Great Britain. As a result, Van Buren faced a succession of diplomatic crises during his four years in office.
In 1837, a Canadian separatist movement attempted to seize independence from Great Britain. When they were unsuccessful, they took refuge in the United States and recruited a number of Americans to support them. The conflict eventually resulted in the death of an American citizen when British loyalists seized and sank a ship supplying the rebels, who based themselves on an island in the Niagara River.
Van Buren sought to avoid escalating tensions with Great Britain, despite domestic calls to declare war. To try and secure a peaceful resolution to the situation, he dispatched General Winfield Scott to the Niagara region to make it clear to any Americans fighting against the British that they would not be supported by the federal government. Also, he declared American neutrality regarding the Canadian independence issue.
While these actions managed to calm the situation, another crisis broke out in 1838, when American and British forces began to clash along a disputed border in northern Maine. To deescalate what was known as the Aroostook War, Van Buren personally agreed with the British minister to the United States to reach a diplomatic solution. He also dispatched General Winfield Scott to calm tensions in the region. Although he had left office by the time of its signing, the 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty resolved the border issues and was the result of the diplomatic process started by Van Buren.

In his posthumously published memoirs, Martin Van Buren covered his rise in New York politics and his subsequent contributions to the formation of the Democratic Party and Andrew Jackson’s presidency. It seems symbolic, however, that the memoirs never reached his own presidential administration, depriving Americans of Van Buren’s self-assessment of his time as chief executive. In much the same way, scholars focus on his pre-presidential enterprises as the peak of his political career, with Van Buren’s presidency a disappointing coda best forgotten.
Van Buren’s life, however, was more than the high of building a political party, more than the low of having his presidential agenda derailed by an economic depression. His story was one of talent, hard work, ambition, success, personal loss, failure, false hope, betrayal, and sadness. In other words, Van Buren lived the range of human experience, making his life a reminder that despite the power and prestige they hold, presidents are regular people, too.
Martin Van Buren was a one-term president whose administration faced significant challenges and produced mixed results at best. His mark on U.S. history was about more than those four years, though. He was the most significant figure in creating the Democratic Party and in setting the expectations for electoral competition based on two opposing political parties. Politics in the United States would look very differently today without his contributions.
texts.1:
#### Politician on the Rise
Born in 1782, Van Buren was the first president born after the American Revolution and the first not descended from the British. He was raised in Columbia County, New York, an area largely populated by people of Dutch ancestry, like the Van Burens, and supportive of the Federalists. Martin’s father, Abraham, was a Jeffersonian Republican, and his son followed in his footsteps.
Martin Van Buren became a lawyer and worked his way up in New York state politics, dominated at the time by the likes of Aaron Burr and DeWitt Clinton. Van Buren spent time in the New York state senate, then was appointed as the state’s attorney general. By the time he entered the U.S. Senate in late 1821, Van Buren had organized an impressive group of New York politicians later dubbed the Albany Regency.
After supporting William H. Crawford’s unsuccessful presidential candidacy in 1824, Van Buren put together a national political coalition that became the Democratic Party. This coalition threw its weight behind Andrew Jackson in 1828, helping him win the presidency. Jackson rewarded Van Buren, recently elected as New York’s governor, by appointing him U.S. secretary of state.
Van Buren proved to be adept at foreign relations. More importantly for his future political career, he was also the president’s staunchest ally in the cabinet. When internal dissension over the marriage of one of Jackson’s cabinet secretaries, Secretary of War John Eaton, threatened to tear the cabinet apart, Van Buren sacrificed his position by resigning. His immediate reward was a diplomatic appointment to London. More important was Jackson’s endorsement to become his vice president if he won reelection in 1832, which Jackson did. This decision positioned Van Buren to succeed him at the end of his second term. Van Buren spent most of his time as vice president advising Jackson on the Bank War, the president’s effort to close the Second Bank of the United States.
texts.2:
#### A Disappointing Presidency
After defeating his Whig opponents in the 1836 presidential election, Van Buren intended to continue enacting Jackson’s political agenda. He was able to do so in some cases. Van Buren oversaw the removal of the Cherokee Indians via the Trail of Tears and persisted in prosecuting the war against the Seminole Indians in Florida. He also continued supporting the institution of slavery in a bid to retain the political support of white southerners. Like Jackson, Van Buren also deferred a decision on the annexation of Texas.
The onset of the 1837 economic depression shortly after Van Buren took office, however, presented him with unexpected challenges. The changed economic circumstances facing the nation forced him to spend considerable time looking for a solution that would provide financial stability. Congress did not implement Van Buren’s proposal—housing federal dollars in an independent Treasury rather than a national bank or state banks—until the last year of his presidency when it passed the Independent Treasury Act of 1840.
Other circumstances provided Van Buren with the opportunity to prove his political acumen as chief executive. Conflicts along the U.S.-Canadian border threatened to ignite a yet another war with Great Britain. Van Buren refused to be provoked into taking aggressive military action, instead relying on diplomacy to defuse the tension. When asked to assist the Mormons in their request for compensation for property lost due to religious persecution, however, Van Buren chose to protect his electoral chances rather than provide them with support.
texts.3:
#### Political Defeat and Retirement
The 1840 presidential campaign exposed Van Buren’s (and the Democratic Party’s) many weaknesses. The Whig Party had spent the years since the last presidential election organizing its members in formidable ways, embracing the cultural politics—material, print, and visual culture, political events and music, public correspondence, auxiliary organizations, and women’s political activity—that Van Buren and many Democrats had never fully activated on a national scale. The Whigs were able to hammer the president on his weak, ineffective response to the economic depression and its effects on the American people.
The Whigs nominated a military hero, William Henry Harrison, and constructed an image of him as an ordinary farmer who understood the plight facing everyday Americans. Meanwhile, they portrayed Van Buren as an out-of-touch elitist living in luxury while average Americans suffered. Neither image was correct—Harrison came from wealth, while Van Buren did not—but in politics, perception often trumps reality.
Although Van Buren lost the 1840 presidential election, he was not yet done with presidential politics. He went into the 1844 Democratic National Convention as the favored candidate, but his opposition to immediately allowing Texas to join the United States sunk his chances of receiving the party’s presidential nomination. Then Van Buren’s attempt to influence President James Polk’s cabinet selections failed, leading to a break between the two men that was never repaired.
Four years later in 1848, the antislavery Free Soil Party nominated Van Buren to head its ticket. It was an odd political partnership given Van Buren’s leadership in the Democratic Party that he had founded and his historical support for slavery, and it showed in the ineffectiveness of his campaign.
Van Buren went back to the Democratic Party after 1848, acting as its elder statesman. With the help of two sons and a daughter-in-law, he worked on his memoirs and a study of U.S. political parties. He died at his home in Kinderhook, New York, in 1862.

Martin Van Buren's tenure as the eighth president of the United States began on March 4, 1837, and ended on March 4, 1841. Van Buren, a Democrat and vice president under Andrew Jackson, took office after defeating multiple Whig Party candidates in the 1836 presidential election. Van Buren's presidency ended following his defeat by Whig candidate William Henry Harrison in the 1840 presidential election.
The central issue facing President Van Buren was the Panic of 1837, a sustained economic downturn that began just weeks into his presidency. Van Buren opposed any direct federal government intervention and cut back federal spending to maintain a balanced budget. He also presided over the establishment of the independent treasury system, a series of government vaults that replaced banks as the repository of federal funds. Van Buren continued the Indian removal policies of the Jackson administration, as thousands of Native Americans were resettled west of the Mississippi River during his presidency. He sought to avoid major tensions over slavery, rejecting the possibility of annexing Texas and appealing the case of _United States v. The Amistad_ to the Supreme Court. In foreign affairs, Van Buren avoided war with Britain despite several incidents, including the bloodless Aroostook War and the _Caroline_ Affair.
Van Buren's inability to deal effectively with the economic depression, combined with the growing political strength of the opposition Whigs, led to his defeat in the 1840 presidential election. His presidency was marked as much by failure and criticism as by success and popular acclaim, and is often ranked as average or below-average by historians. His most lasting achievement was as a political organizer who built the modern Democratic Party and guided it to dominance in the new Second Party System.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole16-1)

## Presidential election of 1836
[edit]
Van Buren had emerged as President Andrew Jackson's preferred successor during the Petticoat affair, and Van Buren won election as vice president in 1832.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson19849%E2%80%9310-2) The two men –charismatic "Old Hickory" and the super-efficient "Sly Fox"—had entirely different personalities but had become an effective team in eight years in office together.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-3) Jackson declined to seek another term in the 1836 presidential election, but he remained influential within the Democratic Party, and he strongly supported Van Buren's candidacy in the 1836 election.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-4) With Jackson's support, Van Buren won the presidential nomination of the 1835 Democratic National Convention without opposition.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-5) Two names were put forward for the vice-presidential nomination: Representative Richard M. Johnson of Kentucky, and former senator William Cabell Rives of Virginia. Though most Southern Democrats favored Rives, Jackson preferred Johnson, and his influence helped lead to Johnson's nomination for the vice presidency.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-5)

## Presidential election of 1836
The newly established Whig Party, a loose coalition bound by mutual opposition to Jackson, sought to prevent Van Buren's victory in the election of 1836. Lacking the party unity or organizational strength to field a single ticket or define a single platform, the Whigs fielded multiple candidates in the hope of forcing a contingent election in the House of Representatives.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-6) Senator Hugh Lawson White of Tennessee, a former Jackson ally, emerged as the major Whig candidate in the South, touting himself as the only Southerner in the race. William Henry Harrison, who had gained notoriety for his service in the Battle of Tippecanoe, edged out Senator Daniel Webster to become the main Whig candidate in the North.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2005448%E2%80%93449-7) The Whig Party campaigned on denouncing Jackson's alleged executive tyranny, and attacked Van Buren as an untrustworthy career politician.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2005449%E2%80%93450-8)
texts.3:
## Presidential election of 1836
Van Buren had to articulate a position on slavery that could win full-throated approval in both the pro-slavery South and the Northern states where slavery was illegal and unpopular. The biggest challenge came in the South, where all Yankees were automatically suspect on the slave question.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-9) Van Buren moved to obtain the support of Southerners by assuring them that he opposed abolitionism and supported the continued existence of slavery in states where it was present.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2007508%E2%80%93509-10) Van Buren did not discuss his own personal beliefs, which held that slavery was immoral, but was sanctioned by the Constitution.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-11) Van Buren's strategy was not to defend his personal position, but to attack abolitionists, who were popular nowhere in the United States. As vice president, he cast the tie-breaking Senate vote in favor of a bill to subject abolitionist mail to state laws, thus ensuring that abolitionist mail would not be circulated in the South. While Southern Whigs cast doubt on his devotion to slavery, his supporters insisted he believed in three things: that Congress could not interfere with slavery in the states, that it would be "impolitic" to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, and that agitation about slavery endangered the union. Van Buren and his supporters realized that to build a viable national party and to maintain the union they had to compromise by accepting slavery. The Democrats created the first modern party, but in doing so consciously removed slavery and abolition from the partisan agenda. More than a decade later, in 1848, Van Buren would become a leading opponent of the extension of slavery in the North while running with the Free Soil Party, but by then he had abandoned any hope of Southern support.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-12)

## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### Early Life and New York Politics
Martin Van Buren was born on December 5, 1782, in Kinderhook, New York, near the end of the American Revolution. As a result, he later became the first U.S. president born after American independence, and the first not born a British subject. His Dutch ancestry also made him the first president of non-British descent.
Van Buren attended school until the age of fourteen before becoming a law clerk in 1796. After completing his law studies in New York City, he gained admission to the bar in 1803. Thereafter, Van Buren returned to Kinderhook, where he opened a successful law practice with his half-brother, James J. Van Alen.
During this time, Van Buren became active in New York politics. Though the Federalists (one of the major political parties of the era) were dominant in New York, Van Buren gravitated towards the views of the rival Democratic-Republicans (the party of Thomas Jefferson). Throughout his political career, he remained committed to Jeffersonian principles of limited government and the protection of states' rights.
Elected to the New York State Senate in 1812, and appointed state Attorney General in 1815, Van Buren found himself in frequent conflict with New York Federalists throughout the 1810s. He nonetheless became a powerful force in state politics and won both praise and criticism for his skill at political maneuvering. Early in the 1820s, Van Buren came to head the **Albany Regency**, a powerful party machine that further increased his power in the state.

## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### National Politics and the Founding of the Democratic Party
In 1821, Van Buren won election to the United States Senate from New York. Despite his junior status, his political acumen quickly allowed him to become a prominent figure in national politics. Van Buren was rapidly appointed to the Senate finance committee, and he soon became chairman of the judiciary committee.
Following the election of John Quincy Adams in 1824, Van Buren became a vocal critic of the President, whom he saw as striving to expand the power of the federal government. With an eye towards the election of 1828, Van Buren worked to unite many different factions of the Democratic-Republican party in support of war hero **Andrew Jackson**. This coalition-building effort ultimately resulted in the election of Jackson in 1828 and marked the beginning of the modern-day **Democratic Party**.

### Martin Van Buren and the Administration of Andrew Jackson
Despite his national profile, Van Buren remained a political force in New York State during the 1820s, and in 1828 he successfully ran for Governor of New York. However, while he assumed the governorship in January 1829, he only held it for a few weeks before being selected by Andrew Jackson to become the Secretary of State.
The years of the Jackson presidency were highly tumultuous, and during his first term, Jackson faced serious divisions within his cabinet. During this time, Van Buren became one of President Jackson's closest advisors and friends. Additionally, as Secretary of State, he had several notable accomplishments. These included gaining reparations from France for property seized during the Napoleonic Wars and negotiating a treaty with the Ottoman Empire that allowed American traders access to the Black Sea.
Eventually, divisions within Jackson's cabinet reached a boiling point. Van Buren devised a scheme whereby he would resign, giving Jackson political cover to remove the rest of his cabinet. Jackson agreed to this plan, but subsequently appointed Van Buren as U.S. Minister to Great Britain in 1831.

## The Presidency of Martin Van Buren: Political Rise and National Contributions
### The Path to the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's first term, one of the major sources of division within the cabinet was Vice-President John C. Calhoun. As a result, as Jackson prepared his reelection campaign in 1832, he selected Van Buren to replace Calhoun as his running mate. Jackson easily won reelection.
As Vice-President, much of Van Buren's focus was on "the Bank War"—the Jackson administration's fight with the Second Bank of the United States. This conflict involved Jackson's desire to prevent the recharter of the Bank, which he felt benefited too few wealthy Americans at the expense of the masses. The Bank War helped to rearrange the American political parties of the era. Jackson's opposition coalesced into the Whig Party, while Jackson and Van Buren continued to play key roles in the shaping of the Democratic Party.
As the election of 1836 approached, Jackson made Van Buren his chosen successor. Van Buren, in turn, made it clear that he intended to continue Jackson's policies. With the support of a by-then well-defined Democratic Party, Van Buren defeated three Whig candidates who ran against him, securing more votes than all three combined.

## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### The Panic of 1837 and the Independent Treasury Act
Almost immediately upon assuming the presidency, Van Buren was confronted with a major economic crisis known as the **Panic of 1837**. While historians still debate the exact cause of the Panic, in large part, it was related to policy actions taken by Jackson during the earlier Bank War.
Desiring to remain true to his belief in the principle of limited government, Van Buren's proposed response to the Panic of 1837 was to establish an independent treasury that he hoped would stabilize the American economy by separating federal funding from state banks. The plan drew strong opposition from both Whigs and Van Buren's own party, the Democrats. Eventually, Congress authorized the creation of a Treasury. However, by the time the Independent Treasury Act of 1840 was passed, the economy had been in a depression for almost four years. This, more than any other factor, cost Van Buren in the election of 1840.

### Other Domestic Affairs During the Presidency of Martin Van Buren
During Jackson's second term, Congress had passed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 to legalize the forcible relocation of all Native American peoples to the west of the Mississippi. Van Buren continued this policy. During his time in office, the federal government both oversaw a forced relocation of the Cherokee people and contended with a major uprising of Seminole peoples in Florida. Both events resulted in the deaths of thousands of Native Americans. Van Buren's handling of the Seminole uprising in particular was criticized as inhumane and contributed to the erosion of his popularity.
Van Buren was also confronted with issues related to sectional tensions over slavery. In 1837, he announced that he would not support the annexation of the Mexican territory of Texas. The annexation of Texas would have brought another state that permitted slavery into the Union, and Van Buren's rejection of that possibility did help to calm temporarily tensions over the issue.

## The Martin Van Buren Presidency: Accomplishments and Major Events
### Foreign Affairs During the Martin Van Buren Presidency
A major source of pressure during the Van Buren administration was American relations with Great Britain. As a result, Van Buren faced a succession of diplomatic crises during his four years in office.
In 1837, a Canadian separatist movement attempted to seize independence from Great Britain. When they were unsuccessful, they took refuge in the United States and recruited a number of Americans to support them. The conflict eventually resulted in the death of an American citizen when British loyalists seized and sank a ship supplying the rebels, who based themselves on an island in the Niagara River.
Van Buren sought to avoid escalating tensions with Great Britain, despite domestic calls to declare war. To try and secure a peaceful resolution to the situation, he dispatched General Winfield Scott to the Niagara region to make it clear to any Americans fighting against the British that they would not be supported by the federal government. Also, he declared American neutrality regarding the Canadian independence issue.
While these actions managed to calm the situation, another crisis broke out in 1838, when American and British forces began to clash along a disputed border in northern Maine. To deescalate what was known as the Aroostook War, Van Buren personally agreed with the British minister to the United States to reach a diplomatic solution. He also dispatched General Winfield Scott to calm tensions in the region. Although he had left office by the time of its signing, the 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty resolved the border issues and was the result of the diplomatic process started by Van Buren.

## The Election of 1840 and Martin Van Buren's Later Years
As the election of 1840 approached, Van Buren faced declining favorability across the country. Many were upset at his handling of the economic crisis, others disagreed with his diplomatic approach to dealing with the British, and still others found fault with his handling of slavery concerns. Indeed, in an attempt to earn the support for pro-slavery voices after his refusal to annex Texas, in 1839 Van Buren's administration supported returning the Africans on trial for engaging in mutiny aboard the slave ship _Amistad_ to Spanish authorities. However, the Supreme Court later ruled that the captives had acted in self-defense and ordered their release.
Van Buren was ultimately defeated overwhelmingly by Whig candidate William Henry Harrison in the election of 1840. Despite this, he attempted to run for president again in the Election of 1844. However, the Democratic Party selected James K. Polk over Van Buren, largely due to Polk's support for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. Van Buren ran again as a candidate from the minor Free-Soil Party in 1848, but received very few votes.
After 1848, he effectively retired from politics and spent his later years touring Europe, writing his memoirs, and spending time with his children and grandchildren at his estate in Kinderhook, New York. With the onset of the Civil War, he supported Abraham Lincoln's decision to fight against the Confederacy, but he died before the war's conclusion, in 1862, at the age of seventy-nine.

## What Did Martin Van Buren Do as President? Legacy and Appraisal
Historians generally consider the Presidency of Martin Van Buren to be a disappointment. His inability to address the Crisis of 1837 in a timely manner greatly eroded his popularity and political capital, and his handling of issues relating to Native Americans has been judged harshly in modern times.
However, despite his failings as president, many historians and political scientists recognize Van Buren as one of the most significant politicians of the 19th century. Throughout his career Van Buren consistently played a critical role in the development of the American political system. This was true in New York, where his construction of the Albany Regency was a major step-forward in party politics, and then nationally, where he played a key role in the formation of the Democratic Party.

In his posthumously published memoirs, Martin Van Buren covered his rise in New York politics and his subsequent contributions to the formation of the Democratic Party and Andrew Jackson’s presidency. It seems symbolic, however, that the memoirs never reached his own presidential administration, depriving Americans of Van Buren’s self-assessment of his time as chief executive. In much the same way, scholars focus on his pre-presidential enterprises as the peak of his political career, with Van Buren’s presidency a disappointing coda best forgotten.
Van Buren’s life, however, was more than the high of building a political party, more than the low of having his presidential agenda derailed by an economic depression. His story was one of talent, hard work, ambition, success, personal loss, failure, false hope, betrayal, and sadness. In other words, Van Buren lived the range of human experience, making his life a reminder that despite the power and prestige they hold, presidents are regular people, too.
Martin Van Buren was a one-term president whose administration faced significant challenges and produced mixed results at best. His mark on U.S. history was about more than those four years, though. He was the most significant figure in creating the Democratic Party and in setting the expectations for electoral competition based on two opposing political parties. Politics in the United States would look very differently today without his contributions.

#### Politician on the Rise
Born in 1782, Van Buren was the first president born after the American Revolution and the first not descended from the British. He was raised in Columbia County, New York, an area largely populated by people of Dutch ancestry, like the Van Burens, and supportive of the Federalists. Martin’s father, Abraham, was a Jeffersonian Republican, and his son followed in his footsteps.
Martin Van Buren became a lawyer and worked his way up in New York state politics, dominated at the time by the likes of Aaron Burr and DeWitt Clinton. Van Buren spent time in the New York state senate, then was appointed as the state’s attorney general. By the time he entered the U.S. Senate in late 1821, Van Buren had organized an impressive group of New York politicians later dubbed the Albany Regency.
After supporting William H. Crawford’s unsuccessful presidential candidacy in 1824, Van Buren put together a national political coalition that became the Democratic Party. This coalition threw its weight behind Andrew Jackson in 1828, helping him win the presidency. Jackson rewarded Van Buren, recently elected as New York’s governor, by appointing him U.S. secretary of state.
Van Buren proved to be adept at foreign relations. More importantly for his future political career, he was also the president’s staunchest ally in the cabinet. When internal dissension over the marriage of one of Jackson’s cabinet secretaries, Secretary of War John Eaton, threatened to tear the cabinet apart, Van Buren sacrificed his position by resigning. His immediate reward was a diplomatic appointment to London. More important was Jackson’s endorsement to become his vice president if he won reelection in 1832, which Jackson did. This decision positioned Van Buren to succeed him at the end of his second term. Van Buren spent most of his time as vice president advising Jackson on the Bank War, the president’s effort to close the Second Bank of the United States.

#### A Disappointing Presidency
After defeating his Whig opponents in the 1836 presidential election, Van Buren intended to continue enacting Jackson’s political agenda. He was able to do so in some cases. Van Buren oversaw the removal of the Cherokee Indians via the Trail of Tears and persisted in prosecuting the war against the Seminole Indians in Florida. He also continued supporting the institution of slavery in a bid to retain the political support of white southerners. Like Jackson, Van Buren also deferred a decision on the annexation of Texas.
The onset of the 1837 economic depression shortly after Van Buren took office, however, presented him with unexpected challenges. The changed economic circumstances facing the nation forced him to spend considerable time looking for a solution that would provide financial stability. Congress did not implement Van Buren’s proposal—housing federal dollars in an independent Treasury rather than a national bank or state banks—until the last year of his presidency when it passed the Independent Treasury Act of 1840.
Other circumstances provided Van Buren with the opportunity to prove his political acumen as chief executive. Conflicts along the U.S.-Canadian border threatened to ignite a yet another war with Great Britain. Van Buren refused to be provoked into taking aggressive military action, instead relying on diplomacy to defuse the tension. When asked to assist the Mormons in their request for compensation for property lost due to religious persecution, however, Van Buren chose to protect his electoral chances rather than provide them with support.

#### Political Defeat and Retirement
The 1840 presidential campaign exposed Van Buren’s (and the Democratic Party’s) many weaknesses. The Whig Party had spent the years since the last presidential election organizing its members in formidable ways, embracing the cultural politics—material, print, and visual culture, political events and music, public correspondence, auxiliary organizations, and women’s political activity—that Van Buren and many Democrats had never fully activated on a national scale. The Whigs were able to hammer the president on his weak, ineffective response to the economic depression and its effects on the American people.
The Whigs nominated a military hero, William Henry Harrison, and constructed an image of him as an ordinary farmer who understood the plight facing everyday Americans. Meanwhile, they portrayed Van Buren as an out-of-touch elitist living in luxury while average Americans suffered. Neither image was correct—Harrison came from wealth, while Van Buren did not—but in politics, perception often trumps reality.
Although Van Buren lost the 1840 presidential election, he was not yet done with presidential politics. He went into the 1844 Democratic National Convention as the favored candidate, but his opposition to immediately allowing Texas to join the United States sunk his chances of receiving the party’s presidential nomination. Then Van Buren’s attempt to influence President James Polk’s cabinet selections failed, leading to a break between the two men that was never repaired.
Four years later in 1848, the antislavery Free Soil Party nominated Van Buren to head its ticket. It was an odd political partnership given Van Buren’s leadership in the Democratic Party that he had founded and his historical support for slavery, and it showed in the ineffectiveness of his campaign.
Van Buren went back to the Democratic Party after 1848, acting as its elder statesman. With the help of two sons and a daughter-in-law, he worked on his memoirs and a study of U.S. political parties. He died at his home in Kinderhook, New York, in 1862.

Martin Van Buren's tenure as the eighth president of the United States began on March 4, 1837, and ended on March 4, 1841. Van Buren, a Democrat and vice president under Andrew Jackson, took office after defeating multiple Whig Party candidates in the 1836 presidential election. Van Buren's presidency ended following his defeat by Whig candidate William Henry Harrison in the 1840 presidential election.
The central issue facing President Van Buren was the Panic of 1837, a sustained economic downturn that began just weeks into his presidency. Van Buren opposed any direct federal government intervention and cut back federal spending to maintain a balanced budget. He also presided over the establishment of the independent treasury system, a series of government vaults that replaced banks as the repository of federal funds. Van Buren continued the Indian removal policies of the Jackson administration, as thousands of Native Americans were resettled west of the Mississippi River during his presidency. He sought to avoid major tensions over slavery, rejecting the possibility of annexing Texas and appealing the case of _United States v. The Amistad_ to the Supreme Court. In foreign affairs, Van Buren avoided war with Britain despite several incidents, including the bloodless Aroostook War and the _Caroline_ Affair.
Van Buren's inability to deal effectively with the economic depression, combined with the growing political strength of the opposition Whigs, led to his defeat in the 1840 presidential election. His presidency was marked as much by failure and criticism as by success and popular acclaim, and is often ranked as average or below-average by historians. His most lasting achievement was as a political organizer who built the modern Democratic Party and guided it to dominance in the new Second Party System.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole16-1)
